messages.content: Write the product page copy for a team chat application, aimed at engineering managers who are choosing between tools. Around 250 words.

# Slate

Every chat tool works fine until the day it doesn't. That day is a Saturday, and something is on fire.

We heard the same story from engineering managers over and over: an incident starts in a DM, moves to a thread two people are following, and lands in the on-call channel forty minutes late, stripped of context. Nothing malfunctioned. The tool just had no opinion about where an incident belongs.

Slate has one. Hit a keystroke on any message and it becomes an incident: new channel, on-call paged off your PagerDuty schedule, the original message pinned at the top, a timestamped log running underneath. Close it and the timeline is already a postmortem draft.

## What you hit in the first week

- Threads with an expiry date. Archive after 14 quiet days, per channel, so search returns decisions rather than debris.
- Stack traces that resolve. Paste one, get file links at the commit your service is actually running.
- Retention you set per channel, exported to S3. Legal stops emailing you.
- SSO, SCIM and audit logs on every tier, the $8 seat included.

## What we left out

No video. No docs. No marketplace of 900 integrations you'll never turn on. If one tool for everything is the goal, buy Teams: cheaper, and already sitting on every laptop.

Our bet is that you'd trade all of that for something that handles the forty minutes after a page.

Free up to 20 seats. Slack history imports in about an hour.

---

Swap in your real numbers for the $8 seat, the 14-day thread expiry, the 20-seat free tier, PagerDuty as the pager, the one-hour Slack import. The copy rests its weight on them, so anything hand-wavy will sag. The competitor line names Teams; rename it or cut it, depending on how hard you want to swing.
Rewrite the text above. Keep the same length and the same purpose. Return only the rewritten text.
